statement: In US adults who had used drugs at least 12 times, in Australian twins and in surveys in 17 countries, starting to use drugs young is associated with more drug problems later (lifetime drug use disorders in the US survey and in the twins, dependence in the 17-country surveys); none of the designs read can show whether starting young itself causes them. In a 1992 US national household survey (NLAES; 42,862 adults interviewed once; about 92% of selected households and 97% of selected people took part), 6,447 people (15.6%, weighted) had used drugs from any of ten classes, other than as prescribed, at least 12 times; 18.6% of them had had lifetime DSM-IV drug dependence and 20.1% drug abuse without dependence. Lifetime dependence was reported by 33.6% of those who recalled first using drugs at 13 or younger, 26.8% at 14, 25.4% at 15, 17.7% at 16 and between 11.4% and 15.1% at 17 or older (13.6% at 21 or older); abuse without dependence fell from 28.9% (13 or younger) to 13.6% (20). After adjustment for age group, sex, race, family history of alcoholism, duration of drug use and current or former use, the odds of lifetime dependence were about 4% lower, and of abuse about 5% lower, for each later year of first use (coefficients −0.04 and −0.05, SE 0.01; the abstract gives the two the other way round). The age of first use was recalled in the same interview as the diagnoses; the drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked; family drug problems, conduct problems and other psychiatric disorders were not measured; current or former use, one of the adjustments, may itself follow from the disorder; and the only prospective study the authors cite, which followed 15-year-old boys for 13 years, found that age at first use did not predict drug-related problems at 30, a result they discount (men only, a single 3-year window, an aggregate measure). The authors call early onset a powerful predictor, but ask whether the delay itself or, more likely, a combination of other factors lowers the risk, and call for prospective studies (Grant & Dawson, 1998). In the young-adult cohort of the volunteer Australian Twin Register (born 1964–1971; telephone interviews in 1996–2000 at a median age of 30; both twins took part in 69% of pairs), in 311 same-sex pairs in which one twin recalled first using cannabis before 17 and the co-twin did not (136 identical and 175 fraternal pairs; 234 co-twins started later and 77 never used cannabis), the twin who started early more often reported any illicit drug abuse or dependence (47.6% against 32.8%; conditional odds ratio 2.24, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.30), cannabis abuse or dependence (45.7% against 31.8%; 2.13, 1.45 to 3.13), alcohol dependence (42.8% against 29.6%; 2.17, 1.46 to 3.24) and use of other drug classes (2.57 to 5.15). Adjustment for differences between co-twins in early tobacco and alcohol use, conduct disorder, depression and social anxiety lowered the odds ratios by up to about a fifth (any drug abuse or dependence 1.98, 1.26 to 3.10; alcohol dependence 1.85, 1.21 to 2.83). Because co-twins grow up in the same home, the association is not explained by what they share; but factors that differ between co-twins, such as friends, were measured only in part and recalled at about 30, identical and fraternal pairs were pooled with no separate estimates for identical pairs, and 311 of the 407 discordant pairs counted in the paper's concordance analysis were analysed, without explanation. The authors read the results as consistent with a causal role and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). In pooled analyses of 17 WHO World Mental Health surveys (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), a later age at first use went with lower odds of later dependence (odds ratios 0.2 to 0.7 across the dependence outcomes, the unit not stated), and using more drug classes with higher odds, while starting drugs in an unusual order was largely unrelated to dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Does starting drugs young go with drug problems later? Yes, in the studies read, but they cannot show that starting young is the cause. In a 1992 US survey of adults who had used drugs at least 12 times, about 1 in 3 of those who started at 13 or younger had been dependent on drugs at some time, against about 1 in 7 of those who started at 21 or older. In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often had a drug problem later than the twin who did not (about 48 in 100 against 33 in 100). Twins grow up in the same home, so the home cannot explain this, but other differences between twins, such as their friends, could, and the study did not show results for identical twins separately. Surveys in 17 countries also linked a younger start with dependence later. All these studies asked adults to remember when they started.

risk_of_bias.note: In both main studies the age of first use and the lifetime diagnoses were reported at the same adult interview, years or decades later, so recall could change the size of the gradient; the survey sampled household survivors and adjusted for current or former use, which may follow from the disorder (card sc_grant_1998: ROBINS-E, high, chiefly for confounding); the twin analysis drew on a volunteer register with 69% pairwise response and used 311 of 407 discordant pairs without explanation (card sc_lynskey_2003: ROBINS-E, high, chiefly for confounding).

inconsistency.note: The same direction in a national survey, a co-twin comparison and 17 cross-national surveys; the survey's per-year gradient is modest and flattens after 17. The one prospective study cited second-hand (Labouvie et al., 1997, young men only) found no prediction; noted, not counted.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: US adults in 1992 who had used drugs at least 12 times, Australian twins born 1964–1971 (early cannabis use) and 17 countries in 2001–2005; outcomes are lifetime diagnoses reported by the participants.

imprecision.note: Large survey samples; the twin odds ratios for drug abuse or dependence, alcohol dependence and other drug use have intervals that exclude 1 (sedative abuse or dependence excepted, not used); the WHO odds ratios have no stated unit and are used only for direction.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the within-pair odds ratios of about 2 shrink with adjustment and could be produced by differences between co-twins.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the survey's gradient is the exposure itself (age at first use), not an amount of drug, and it flattens after 17.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one for risk of bias (recall of onset and diagnoses at one interview in both main studies, with selection in the survey and unexplained losses of discordant twin pairs): very low. The claim is worded as an association and rated as such; whether starting young causes drug use disorders is not rated: the survey cannot separate cause from shared liability, as its authors say, and the co-twin comparison removes what twins share but not what differs between them, nor does it show identical pairs separately. Status replicated: three independent samples (NLAES 1992; the Australian Twin Register; 17 WHO surveys, which do not include NLAES) point the same way. The drug first used and the drug of the disorder are not linked in the survey, and the twin study's exposure is cannabis; the alcohol counterpart from the same survey (Grant & Dawson, 1997) is in the answer on drinking young.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis makes people more likely to go on to other illegal drugs (the 'gateway' idea), or whether the usual order of first use, and the link between the two, come from a shared liability to use drugs and from which drugs people are offered first. In the studies read, cannabis use usually came before other illegal drugs, except where cannabis was rare, and went with a much higher chance of using them. In New York State public high schools in 1971–1973 (5,468 students linked over 5 to 6 months, 66% of the students surveyed in the fall; students who could not be linked had used more drugs), 26% of the 558 students whose drug use had reached cannabis went on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, mostly pills (12 percentage points) or psychedelics (9), with heroin about 2, against 4% of 2,911 students who had used only legal drugs and 1% of 482 who had used none; 56% stayed at cannabis and 19% used only legal drugs in the interval. These percentages were not adjusted for anything; the abstract calls cannabis a crucial step towards other illegal drugs, while the text says a drug does not invariably lead to the next and that the stages are probably culturally determined (Kandel, 1975). In four US household surveys (1991–1994; 44,624 people aged 12 to 25; ages recalled in whole years; people compared within neighbourhood and survey year, with sex, race or ethnicity and age group adjusted for, but no measure of individual liability), people who had used cannabis were more likely to have had a first chance to try cocaine (relative risk 4.6, 95% CI 3.8 to 5.6, without alcohol or tobacco use; 7.6, 6.9 to 8.4, with it; against people who had used none of the three) and, once offered, about 15 times as likely to start (11.3 to 19.8), also when the 73% who started in the same year as their first offer were left out (20.4, 10.2 to 40.7); about half of the people who had used cannabis started cocaine within 2 years of a first offer, against under 10% of the others many years later (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). In Australian twins born 1964–1971 (311 same-sex pairs in which one twin, but not the other, recalled first using cannabis before 17; interviewed at about 30), the twin who started early more often reported later use of other drugs (for example cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% against 26.4%, conditional odds ratio 4.19, 95% CI 2.60 to 6.75; hallucinogens 5.15; sedatives 2.83; opioids 2.57); the odds ratios stayed between 2.3 and 5.2 after adjustment for measured differences between the twins, and between 2.3 and 3.9 (unadjusted) in the 234 pairs in which both twins had used cannabis. The link is therefore not explained by what co-twins share, such as their upbringing; but identical and fraternal pairs were pooled, with no separate estimates for identical pairs, and differences between co-twins such as their friends were not measured; the authors call the results consistent with a causal role, perhaps through the social setting of cannabis use and access to other drugs, and say that strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn from them alone (Lynskey et al., 2003). A simulation of US young people, calibrated to household surveys of 1982–1994, in which one shared liability brings forward both the chances to use and the use of all drugs and cannabis has no effect by design, produced a strong relative risk of using heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens after cannabis (157, against 24 in the surveys), an order in which those drugs rarely come first (11 per 1,000, against 16 in the surveys) and a rise with cannabis frequency, and adjusting for an imperfect measure of that liability left large associations; it shows that these patterns cannot by themselves identify a cause, but it was not compared with a model that includes one, and its authors think something like a gateway effect probably exists through contact with illegal markets (Morral et al., 2002). In 17 WHO surveys (2001–2005; ages recalled at one interview), the order depended on how common each drug was: other illegal drugs came before cannabis in 11.4% (USA) and 12.7% (New Zealand) of people who had used them by 29, against 83.2% in Japan and 77.8% in Nigeria, where cannabis was rare (13 of 16 and 7 of 8 people); the link of cannabis with later other drug use was weaker where cannabis was more common, while that of alcohol or tobacco with later other drug use was stronger where those were more common; and starting in an unusual order was largely unrelated to later dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). A narrative review by proponents of a shared liability argues that the order need not reflect causal steps and calls that liability empirically proven, but does not discuss the co-twin evidence (Vanyukov et al., 2012). No study read separated a causal effect, a shared liability and access to drugs in one design, and all their data were collected between 1971 and 2005. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs? This is not known. In most places studied, most people who used other illegal drugs had used cannabis first, and people who had used cannabis were more likely to go on to other drugs: in New York schools in the early 1970s, about 1 in 4 students who had used cannabis tried another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, against 4 in 100 of those who had used only alcohol or tobacco. In Australian twins, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often used other drugs later than the other twin, so the home they shared does not explain it, but other differences between the twins could. A computer model showed that the same pattern appears if some people are simply more likely to use any drug and are offered cannabis first, with no effect of cannabis at all. In surveys in 17 countries the order depended on how common each drug was: where cannabis was rare, most people who used other drugs had not used it first, though very few people were involved. No study separated cause, shared risk and access to drugs. See the contested question.

risk_of_bias.note: No individual liability was measured in the school panel or the surveys (cards sc_kandel_1975: ROBINS-E, very high, no adjustment at all and a third of the panel lost, more of them people who used drugs; sc_wagner_2002 and sc_degenhardt_2010a: high); the co-twin study cannot exclude factors that differ between co-twins and shows no identical-pair estimates (sc_lynskey_2003: high); the simulation's assumptions are untested and it was not compared with a model that includes a gateway effect (sc_morral_2002: high); the review is an argued position without search or appraisal (sc_vanyukov_2012: high).

inconsistency.note: The strength of the link varies widely between countries (cannabis and later other illegal drugs at 18–29, odds ratio 7.4 in the Netherlands against 107.1 in the USA), the order reverses where cannabis is rare, and the designs point different ways on cause: a co-twin comparison finds a link beyond shared family factors, while a model with no effect of cannabis reproduces the population patterns.

indirectness.note: All data were collected between 1971 and 2005, mostly in the USA and Australia; the cross-national surveys show that the pattern depends on place and time, so it may differ in other places and in later years, including where cannabis is sold legally (not studied in the papers read).

imprecision.note: Large surveys and twin intervals that exclude 1; the Japan and Nigeria proportions rest on 16 and 8 people and are used only to show that the order can differ; the simulation gives no intervals.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence and a simulation start low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low, the floor. The claim concerns cause, so its relation is insufficient evidence; that cannabis use usually comes first and goes with a higher chance of using other illegal drugs is reported in it, not rated as a separate claim. Counted once: Wagner & Anthony (1991–1994) and Morral et al. (1982–1994) draw on the same series of US household surveys; Vanyukov et al. add no data and cite Morral et al. and Degenhardt, Dierker, et al.; the WHO surveys include the US and New Zealand surveys whose earlier analyses the paper cites. Status contested: a co-twin comparison and survey analyses point to a link beyond shared family factors and beyond being offered, while a model and cross-national data show that a shared liability and access can produce the same patterns, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does using cannabis make people more likely to go on to other illegal drugs, or do the usual order and the link come from a shared liability to use drugs and from which drugs people are offered first?
debate.evidence_yes: In Australian twins born 1964–1971, the twin who started cannabis before 17 more often went on to use other drugs than the co-twin who did not (conditional odds ratios 2.57 to 5.15; for example cocaine or other stimulants 47.9% against 26.4%), also after adjustment for measured differences between the twins (2.3 to 5.2) and in pairs in which both twins had used cannabis (2.3 to 3.9); a comparison within pairs removes everything co-twins share, including their upbringing (Lynskey et al., 2003). In US household surveys of 1991–1994, people who had used cannabis were more likely to be offered cocaine (relative risks 4.6 to 7.6) and, once offered, about 15 times as likely to start, also when people who started in the same year as the offer were left out (20.4), with people compared within the same neighbourhood and survey year (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). Cannabis came before other illegal drugs for most people in most places studied; in 1971–1973 about a quarter of New York State students at the cannabis step went on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months, against 4% of students who had used only legal drugs (Kandel, 1975); and in nearly every one of 17 countries, starting a drug earlier in the usual sequence went with much higher odds of starting a later one (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). Routes proposed but not tested include the social setting in which cannabis is used, lower perceived risk, and access to other drugs through people who sell cannabis (Lynskey et al., 2003; Morral et al., 2002).
debate.evidence_no: A simulation in which one shared liability, and the order in which drugs are offered, drive all first use, with no effect of cannabis by design, reproduced the patterns usually cited for a gateway: a strong relative risk (157 in the model against 24 in US surveys), an order in which heroin, cocaine or hallucinogens rarely come first (11 against 16 per 1,000) and a rise with cannabis frequency; adjusting for an imperfect measure of that liability left large associations (an odds ratio of 297 fell only to 82 with a measure of reliability 0.8), so adjustment of the kind used in observational studies cannot rule a shared liability out (Morral et al., 2002). Across 17 countries the order depended on how common each drug was: where cannabis was rare (Japan, Nigeria), most people who used other illegal drugs had not used cannabis first, though from very few people; the link of cannabis with later other drug use was weaker where cannabis was common; and starting out of order did not go with more dependence (Degenhardt, Dierker, et al., 2010). In 1971–1973, most New York State students at the cannabis step did not move on within 5 to 6 months (56% stayed at cannabis, 19% used only legal drugs in the interval), the author wrote that the stages are probably culturally determined, and nothing was adjusted for (Kandel, 1975). The US survey analysis places part of the link at being offered cocaine, which fits access as well as an effect of cannabis, and measured no individual liability (Wagner & Anthony, 2002). Proponents of a shared liability argue that the order follows how available and common each drug is and that the stages are defined circularly (Vanyukov et al., 2012).
debate.neither_can_show: Nobody can be assigned to use cannabis at random. The school panel and the household surveys rest on self-reports, mostly ages recalled years later in whole years, and measured no individual liability; the co-twin design removes what twins share but not what differs between them (friends, temperament, their own early behaviour), and the study read shows no separate results for identical twins; a simulation shows what a model can produce, not what happened. The cross-national comparison rests on differences between countries that also differ in law, drug markets and willingness to report use. None of the designs separates an effect of cannabis itself from the effect of buying it where other drugs are sold, and all the data were collected between 1971 and 2005.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). That cannabis use usually comes before other illegal drugs, and goes with a much higher chance of using them, is found in every study read, except where cannabis was rare; that a shared liability and the order in which drugs are offered can produce this pattern without any effect of cannabis is shown by a model; and that the link persists within twin pairs shows that the family background twins share does not explain all of it. The evidence read cannot say whether the remaining link is an effect of cannabis, of access to illegal markets, or of differences between twins, and in the one study that followed students over a few months, about 3 in 4 students at the cannabis step did not move on to another illegal drug within 5 to 6 months.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A cohort followed from before any drug use, recording offers and first use of each drug as they happen, with liability measured beforehand (behaviour, family and friends' use) and the local availability of each drug, and with enough identical twin pairs who differ in cannabis use to give separate estimates; and natural experiments that change access to cannabis without changing access to other drugs, such as legal sales kept apart from illegal markets, with later use of other drugs measured.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether a richer, shared living space makes animals take less of a drug, and these animal studies cannot show anything about people. In three small experiments from one laboratory (Simon Fraser University; 1978, 1979 and 1981; the original papers are not read here and are described by a critical history), rats housed together in a large enclosure with sawdust, boxes and tubes ('Rat Park') drank less morphine solution than rats housed alone in small cages, but only under particular conditions: on choice days after a period of forced morphine drinking (1978), with sweetened, weak solutions (1979), and according to the housing at the time of testing, not in early life (1981). During 57 days when morphine solution was their only fluid, the Rat Park rats drank more on average (18.6 against 13.3 mg of morphine hydrochloride per rat, as tabulated), and they did drink morphine, contrary to popular accounts. The groups held 8 to 22 rats, males and females lived together in Rat Park with no account of pregnancies, intake was measured by different methods in the two housing conditions, and the many comparisons raised the risk of chance findings; the original authors drew cautious conclusions and did not link the results to drug problems in people (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). Two experiments designed to repeat the 1981 study, each with 10 male and 10 female rats in each housing condition, did not find lower intake in colony rats: in the first, colony rats drank slightly more of the strongest solution (3.6 against 0.0 g a day) and no differently at the three weaker ones; in the second, with the colony's intake known only as a group total and no statistical test, isolated rats drank more at three of four strengths, by smaller margins than the up to sevenfold difference described for 1981 (Petrie, 1996). The author's explanation, a change in the supplier's breeding stock, was not tested, and this study too measured intake differently in the two housing conditions. Other housing studies, summarized second-hand, point both ways: in one, rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake and the enriched rats drank more cocaine solution; in another, isolated rats quickly learned to give themselves intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In a different kind of experiment, male rats offered a choice between an intravenous cocaine infusion and a sweet drink almost all came to prefer the sweet drink, also after a period of escalating cocaine intake and while under the influence of cocaine, though they still chose cocaine on about 16% of choices (Lenoir et al., 2007); earlier studies in monkeys, as those authors note, found most monkeys preferring high doses of cocaine to food. Every finding here comes from animals under laboratory conditions; how housing, poverty, opportunity or social exclusion shape drug use and drug problems in people is not shown by these designs. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: What did the 'Rat Park' studies show about environment and drugs? Less than is often said, and only in rats. In the Rat Park studies of 1978 to 1981, rats living together in a big space with things to do drank less morphine water than rats kept alone, but only in some conditions; when morphine water was all they had to drink, the Rat Park rats drank more. The groups were small, and drinking was measured in different ways for the two groups. Two later experiments meant to repeat the 1981 study did not find less drinking in rats living together. In a different kind of study, rats almost always chose a sweet drink over cocaine. None of this tested people, so it cannot say how where people live shapes their drug use. See the contested question.
population: Laboratory rats: Wistar rats in the three Rat Park experiments of 1978–1981 (groups of 8 to 22; as described by Gage & Sumnall, 2019); 80 outbred Wistar rats of both sexes in two repeat experiments (Petrie, 1996); male Wistar rats in cocaine-choice experiments (Lenoir et al., 2007); no people
exposure: Housing together in a large enclosure or colony box from weaning or at testing ('Rat Park'); in the choice experiments, a sweet drink (saccharin or sucrose water) available as an alternative to cocaine
comparator: Rats housed alone in small standard cages; in the choice experiments, rats offered only the cocaine lever, or water instead of the sweet drink
outcome: Voluntary intake of oral morphine solution (sweetened or not) beside water; choice of intravenous cocaine infusions against the alternative
magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of environment. Rat Park, as tabulated by Gage & Sumnall (2019): 1978, forced access (57 days) Rat Park 18.6 vs isolated 13.3 mg morphine hydrochloride per rat; Nichols cycles F = 200.9 (df 1/69) and abstinence period F 26.38 (df 1/23), isolated rats drinking more on choice days; 1979, housing difference only with 10% sucrose, largest at 0.15 mg/ml; 1981, housing at testing F = 33.64, p < 0.0001 (df not printed). Petrie (1996), isolated vs colony, grams of morphine solution a day: Experiment 1, 1.0 mg/ml 0.0 vs 3.6 (colony more; F(1, 34) = 80.98 for grams), 0.5 mg/ml 0.5 vs 1.3, 0.25 mg/ml 15.7 vs 18.3, 0.125 mg/ml 30.2 vs 42.8 (no housing difference at these three); Experiment 2 (no test), 0.3 vs 4.3, 9.4 vs 3.0, 17.4 vs 10.9, 44.4 vs 33.1; the 1981 difference described as up to sevenfold. Lenoir et al. (2007), male rats, intravenous cocaine (0.25 mg per infusion, study condition) vs 20 s of 0.2% saccharin: saccharin preferred from day 2 (N = 43); rats preferring cocaine 2.3% (drug-naive), 8.3% (first trained on cocaine), none of 11 (after intake escalated from 7.34 to 26.04 mg/day); cocaine chosen on about 15.6% of choices on average.

risk_of_bias.note: Animal experiments without described random allocation, with unblinded weighing by different methods in the two housing conditions (card sc_petrie_1996: SYRCLE high); the choice experiments had no random allocation and excluded 15% of rats, mostly from the cocaine-only condition (card sc_lenoir_2007: SYRCLE high); the original Rat Park experiments cannot be appraised from a second-hand history and share the measurement problem.

inconsistency.note: The original experiments and the direct repeat point in opposite directions, the repeat's two experiments disagree with each other in three of four morphine phases, and the other housing studies summarized point both ways.

indirectness.note: Preclinical evidence is always indirect: oral morphine drinking beside water, or a few intravenous cocaine infusions a day in a choice procedure, in one rat strain; cage against colony box is a narrow stand-in for an environment. Rated as worded, for animals; the statement says that nothing about people can be shown.

imprecision.note: Groups of 8 to 22 rats in the originals and 10 per sex and housing condition in the repeat, no standard deviations, and one repeat experiment without any test.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; one published repeat attempt is known from the sources read.

grade.reasoning: Animal experiments without described random allocation start low (the original Rat Park papers are seen only through a critical history, which adds to the risk of bias because they cannot be appraised). Down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. The relation is insufficient evidence: a housing effect on drug intake in rats is neither shown nor excluded. Status contested: the original findings and the direct repeat point in opposite directions, and a credible published critique changes how the originals should be read (METHODS 6.4), so the six-part box applies. The choice experiments of Lenoir et al. (2007) answer a different question (a sweet drink against cocaine) and are kept apart from the housing evidence; their preference is consistent within one procedure, one strain and one sex, and earlier monkey studies point the other way. The critical history misattributes Petrie's repeat to the 1979 study (card reporting issue); the statement names the 1981 study, as Petrie does. Petrie (1996) gives no dates for its experiments, so the repeat is dated by its publication.

debate.question: Does a richer, shared living space make rats take less morphine or cocaine, as the 'Rat Park' story says, and what can such studies say about people?
debate.evidence_yes: In the three Rat Park experiments, as summarized by a critical history, isolated rats drank more morphine solution than colony rats on choice days in the later periods of the 1978 study (Nichols cycles, F = 200.9, df 1/69; abstinence period, F 26.38, df 1/23; both p < 0.001), with sweetened weak solutions in morphine-naive rats in 1979 (largest difference at 0.15 mg/ml with 10% sucrose), and in 1981 according to the housing at the time of testing, whatever the early housing (F = 33.64, p < 0.0001) (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In the second experiment of the repeat, isolated rats drank more of three of the four morphine solutions (for example 44.4 against 33.1 g a day at the weakest), the direction of the original finding, though without a test (Petrie, 1996). As summarized second-hand, isolated rats quickly learned to give themselves intravenous cocaine while socially housed rats did not consistently (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In choice experiments, almost every male rat came to prefer a sweet drink to intravenous cocaine, across the cocaine doses, delays and costs tested, after escalating intake and during intoxication (2.3% of drug-naive rats, 8.3% of rats first trained on cocaine and none of 11 rats with escalated intake preferred cocaine) (Lenoir et al., 2007). The critical history still calls the core message, that drug problems are more than a biological response to a drug, important (Gage & Sumnall, 2019).
debate.evidence_no: In the 1978 experiment, Rat Park rats drank more morphine than isolated rats during the 57 days when it was their only fluid (18.6 against 13.3 mg per rat, as tabulated), and isolated rats drank less on non-choice days; in 1979 there was little evidence of a housing difference at high morphine and low sugar concentrations; differences appeared only in specific conditions and stages; intake was measured with different methods in the two housing conditions, groups were very small, males and females shared the colony, and many comparisons were made (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). The two experiments designed to repeat the 1981 study did not find lower intake in colony rats: in the first, with a statistical test, colony rats drank slightly more of the strongest solution (3.6 against 0.0 g a day) and no differently at the weaker ones, and no difference in either experiment came near the up to sevenfold difference described for 1981 (Petrie, 1996). As summarized second-hand, rats reared in enriched or impoverished conditions did not differ in morphine intake, and the enriched rats drank more cocaine solution (Gage & Sumnall, 2019). In earlier choice studies, most monkeys preferred high doses of cocaine to food, in one study to a sucrose pellet, as Lenoir et al. (2007) note, and the rats' preference for a sweet drink was shown in one strain, one sex and one procedure with eight choices a day.
debate.neither_can_show: None of these studies measured anything in people: a cage against a colony box is a narrow stand-in for a human environment, oral morphine drinking or a few cocaine infusions a day is not human drug use, and housing, poverty, opportunity, social exclusion and access to services, which matter for people, were not studied. Even for rats, measuring intake by different methods in the two housing conditions (in the originals and in the repeat) means that part of any difference could come from the measuring; the explanation offered for the failed repeat (a change in the rats' breeding stock) was not tested; and no study read here allocated rats to housing at random and measured intake the same way in both groups.
debate.editors_reading: The editors' reading: the popular account, that rats in a rich environment refuse morphine, is not what the original papers reported, since Rat Park rats did drink morphine and drank more of it when it was their only fluid. The housing effect rests on three small experiments from one laboratory with a built-in measurement difference, and the one direct repeat did not reproduce it, so whether housing changes drug taking in rats is not settled; certainty very low. That a sweet drink can win over cocaine in a choice procedure is a separate rat finding, consistent within one procedure but contradicted by earlier monkey studies. For people, these studies can only suggest questions; the evidence in people is of other kinds (see the answers on recovery from drug and alcohol problems and on whether people choose other rewards over cocaine).
debate.what_would_settle_it: For rats: a preregistered, adequately powered replication with random allocation to colony or isolated housing, the same automated individual measurement of intake in both conditions, both sexes housed so that litters cannot occur, blinded analysis and more than one strain or supplier. For people: longitudinal or natural-experiment studies of how housing, opportunity and social exclusion change the course of drug use.
